# The Encrypted Key-Value Store

FOKS stores files for users and teams in a directory tree that lives on a
server. The server must be able to store the tree, hand back any part of it
on request, page through a large directory, and reject a write that would
clobber a concurrent one. It must not be able to learn the names of files or
directories, the contents of files, or, as far as practical, the shape of the
tree. And when a member is removed from a team, the keys that protect the
tree must change without re-encrypting every byte the team has ever stored.

Four techniques meet these requirements: a three-level key hierarchy, a
keyed hash beside a randomised encryption of every name, position-derived
nonces, and optimistic concurrency in which every write states what it read.

## Cryptographic file systems on untrusted storage

Plutus (Kallahalla et al., 2003) and SiRiUS (Goh et al.,
2003) both put encrypted files on a server that is trusted to store bytes but
not to keep them secret or to leave them alone, and both separate the key
that protects a file's *contents* from the keys that protect its metadata and
its directory. Keybase's KBFS, the most direct ancestor of the FOKS design,
also encrypts file and directory names: the server holds a tree whose nodes
it can address but not read.

A server that cannot read names also cannot answer "does this directory
contain `config.toml`?" The client must either download the whole directory
and search locally, or give the server something it *can* compare: a
deterministic encoding of the name, so that the same name in the same
directory always encodes to the same bytes. Bellare, Boldyreva and O'Neill
(2007) formalised what such *deterministic encryption* can offer: it hides
everything except equality, and only when the values come from a
distribution the attacker cannot enumerate. A file name is a short,
low-entropy string, so a deterministic encoding under a public key would be
guessable. FOKS avoids this by using a *keyed* function whose key the server
does not have.

## The key hierarchy

Every KV namespace belongs to a *party*: a user or a team, identified by a
party ID and a host ID. The party's shared key (a PUK for a user, a PTK for a
team; see [Chapter 5](05-generations.qmd)) exists in generations, and every
object in the store names the role and generation of the key that protects
it. From one exact seed the client derives a *KV keyset* of two 32-byte keys
by the typed-HMAC scheme of [Chapter 3](03-key-hierarchy.qmd):

| Step | Derivation |
|---|---|
| Application key | `derive_key(seed, 5)` |
| KV application key | `HMAC(app_key, APP_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID ‖ encode([0, "0" → 0]))` |
| MAC key | `HMAC(kv_app, KV_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID ‖ encode([1, nil]))` |
| Box key | `HMAC(kv_app, KV_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID ‖ encode([2, nil]))` |

Every HMAC is HMAC-SHA-512/256 over a 64-bit type ID followed by the
canonically encoded object, and every symmetric encryption is a *typed
secretbox*: XSalsa20-Poly1305 with a 24-byte nonce formed from the 8-byte type
ID and a 16-byte partial nonce that the caller supplies. The type ID in the
nonce means that two ciphertexts of different kinds can never be swapped for
one another even if their keys and partial nonces coincide.

The party keyset is used sparingly: it authenticates the root and seals
seeds and small files. Everything else is protected by a directory's or a
file's own seed:

```
party seed (PUK/PTK, role r, generation g)
  └─ KV keyset {mac, box}
       ├─ root binding MAC
       ├─ directory seed  (32 random bytes, sealed under box key)
       │    └─ directory keyset {mac, box}
       │         ├─ dirent name MAC        (deterministic)
       │         ├─ dirent name box        (randomised)
       │         └─ dirent binding MAC
       ├─ small-file box
       └─ file seed  (32 random bytes, sealed under box key)
            └─ chunk encryption
```

The reason for three levels is rotation. When a team member is removed the
PTK advances to a new generation ([Chapter 5](05-generations.qmd)). If every
name and chunk were encrypted directly under the PTK, the whole store would
have to be rewritten; instead only the seed boxes need re-sealing, one per
directory and one per large file. A `KvDirectoryPair` can hold both an
`Active` directory record and an `Encrypting` one under a newer generation;
the client opens one seed per generation and picks the seed an entry was
written under by its `directory_version`. A third status, `Dead`, also
exists.

## The root

The root of a namespace is a small record: a 16-byte directory ID, a version
number, the role and generation of the party key, and a 32-byte *binding
MAC* computed under the party's MAC key over `[party, key, root id,
version]`. Because the party (ID and host ID) is inside the MAC, a server
cannot present one user's root as another's; because the version is inside
it, a server cannot roll a namespace back to an older root. The client
verifies the MAC under the generation the root names before following it.

A namespace is created lazily: the first write creates a directory with a
random ID and seed, then puts a root pointing at it, and if two devices race
one directory becomes unreferenced garbage. Reads never create a namespace.
A missing root is an empty store only if the client has never seen a root
for that party; otherwise it is an error, because the disappearance of a
known root is what a rollback looks like.

## Directories and entries

A directory record holds its ID, version, party key reference, the sealed
seed, a `write_role` (the minimum role that may write into it), and its
status. The seed is sealed under the party's box key with the directory ID as
the partial nonce, so a seed ciphertext moved to another directory ID fails
to open.

A directory *entry* (dirent) is the record that maps a name to a node:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parent` | 16-byte ID of the containing directory |
| `id` | 16-byte random dirent ID |
| `value` | 17-byte node ID: one type byte plus 16 random bytes |
| `version` | this dirent's version, starting at 1 |
| `directory_version` | version of the parent when the entry was written |
| `write_role` | minimum role that may replace this entry |
| `name_mac` | deterministic keyed hash of the name |
| `name_box` | randomised encryption of the name |
| `directory_status` | the parent's status at write time |
| `binding_mac` | MAC over all client-authored fields |
| `creation_time` | assigned by the server |

The node type byte distinguishes `None` (0, a tombstone), `Directory` (1),
`File` (2, a chunked large file), `SmallFile` (3) and `Symlink` (4). A dirent
points at a node ID; the node is fetched separately, which is what makes
`mv` cheap: moving an entry changes dirents, not nodes.

## Two encodings of every name

The central technique of the store is that each name is stored twice under
the directory's keyset. Let `payload = encode([parent, directory_version,
name])`. Then:

```
name_mac = HMAC(dir_mac_key, KV_DIRENT_NAME_PAYLOAD_TYPE_ID ‖ payload)
name_box = secretbox(dir_box_key, nonce = type ‖ random16, pad(payload))
```

The MAC is *deterministic*: a given name in a given directory at a given
directory version always produces the same 32 bytes. A client that holds the
directory seed can compute the MAC of a candidate name and ask the server for
exactly that entry, and the server can index entries by MAC, sort them, and
page through them in MAC order. The box is *randomised*: a fresh 16-byte nonce makes two boxes of the same
name unrelated, and it exists so that a listing can recover plaintext names,
which a MAC alone cannot. The box's plaintext is padded to a power of two (at least 32 bytes) so
its length reveals only a bucket, not the exact name length.

Both encodings contain the parent ID and the directory version. On open the
client decrypts the box, re-encodes canonically, verifies the name MAC and
the dirent's `binding_mac`, and checks that the parent and version inside
the plaintext equal the dirent's own fields, which catches a dirent copied
from another directory or replayed from an older version of this one. The
binding MAC covers `(parent, id, value, version, directory_version,
write_role, name_mac, name_box)`, so the server also cannot repoint a name
at a different node or change the role needed to overwrite it. The one
field outside it, `creation_time`, is the field the server sets.

### What the server learns

Deterministic encryption trades some secrecy for searchability. The MAC key
is per directory, derived from a seed the server never sees, and the MAC
payload includes the directory version. So:

- The server learns equality of names within one directory at one directory
  version. The directory version changes only when the directory record is
  re-keyed, not on every write, so the server can tell that a name unlinked
  and later recreated in the same directory is the same name, and that a
  lookup by MAC targets an entry it has seen before. Among live entries this
  reveals nothing new, because names within a directory are unique.
- The server cannot tell whether two entries in *different* directories
  share a name, because different directories have unrelated MAC keys.
- The server cannot run a dictionary attack on names, because it lacks the
  key; this is what makes a deterministic encoding safe for low-entropy
  names.
- The server learns the *access pattern*: which directory IDs a client
  fetches, in what order, and how many entries each has. It also sees the
  padded size of every name box, small file and chunk, so sizes are known to
  within a power-of-two bucket. FOKS does not attempt to hide this; hiding
  access patterns would require oblivious RAM, at a cost out of proportion
  to the threat.

The MAC also serves as the *pagination cursor*. A listing returns at most
100 entries ordered by `(name_mac, dirent_id)`, and the client asks for the
next page with the last MAC it saw. This is keyset rather than offset
pagination, so a concurrent insert cannot cause an entry to be skipped or
repeated, and the order is opaque to the server. The client re-sorts by
plaintext name after decrypting. Tombstones (type byte zero) are excluded
from listings, so a deleted name costs a reader nothing.

## Path lookup

The server never receives a path. To resolve `/a/b/c` the client fetches and
verifies the root, lists the root directory, decrypts names until it finds
`a`, checks that `a` is a directory, and repeats. Two traversal plans exist:
a *path walk* that visits one directory per component, and a *complete*
breadth-first traversal over every reachable directory, with a visited set
and the protocol's directory limit as a cap. Every decrypted name is
validated (UTF-8, no NUL, no `/`, not `.` or `..`, unique within the
directory) before it is trusted. Symlink targets are stored as encrypted
small-file payloads and returned to the caller rather than followed; only
the adapter's whole-tree resolver follows them. Paths are absolute, at most
4,096 bytes, with components of 1 to 255 bytes.

## Files: small, large, and chunked

A file is small if it fits in one upload read and is at most 2,040 bytes. It is one typed secretbox under the
party's box key with the node's random, single-use object ID as partial
nonce, and its plaintext is padded to a power of two. A symlink is the same
box with a different tag inside the plaintext.

Anything larger is a chunked file:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Maximum plaintext per upload chunk | 4 MiB |
| Maximum file size | 1 GiB |
| Maximum chunks read per file | 4,096 |
| File seed | 32 random bytes, sealed in the file's metadata |
| Chunk cipher | XSalsa20-Poly1305 under the file seed |
| Chunk nonce | first 24 bytes of `hash(KV_CHUNK_NONCE_PAYLOAD_TYPE_ID, encode([object_id, offset, final]))` |

The file seed is sealed under the party's box key together with the node's
object ID and the metadata version, and both are checked on open, so a seed
cannot be transplanted between files. Chunk plaintexts are padded to a
power-of-two bucket plus the encoding header, and the padding must be all
zeros on decryption.

### Why deterministic nonces are safe here

Ordinarily a nonce is chosen at random, because reusing a nonce with the
same key under a stream cipher leaks the XOR of two plaintexts. The chunk
nonce is a hash of `(object ID, byte offset, is-final flag)`. It is safe for
two reasons. First, the key is unique to the file, and within one file each
`(offset, final)` pair is encrypted exactly once, so no `(key, nonce)` pair
repeats. Second, making the nonce a function of position turns a class of
attacks into decryption failures. A server that answers a request for the
chunk at offset 4 MiB with the chunk at offset 8 MiB cannot succeed: the
client derives the nonce from the offset it *asked for*, and the
authentication tag fails. Before decrypting, the client also checks that the
offset stated in the chunk record equals the one it requested. As Rogaway's treatment of
nonce-based encryption makes clear, a nonce need only be unique, not
unpredictable, and choosing it from context authenticates the context for
free.

The last chunk carries the total encrypted size. The dirent that links the
node into a directory is written only after the last chunk, so a crash
mid-upload leaves an unreferenced node, never a name that points at half a
file.

The Rust implementation seals one extra field into the metadata's opaque
custom area: the plaintext length. For Go-written files without it, the
client measures the length on first download, stores it locally keyed on
the node ID, and treats a later mismatch as an integrity error.

## Optimistic concurrency with version vectors

Two devices or two team members may write to the same directory at once. FOKS uses optimistic concurrency control (Kung and
Robinson, 1981): a writer does not lock; it states what it believes the
current state to be, and the server rejects the write if that belief is
stale. The everyday form of this idea is HTTP's `If-Match` header with an
entity tag.

The belief is a *version vector*: the root version, and for each directory
the write depends on, that directory's version and the `(dirent id, version)`
of every dirent the writer listed there. The server compares the vector with
its current heads and, if anything cited has moved, returns a stale-cache
error listing only the objects whose versions are newer. The client refreshes
those, re-prepares, and retries, up to three attempts.

Two details make the vector trustworthy. First, it cites dirent *IDs*, not
just names and versions: a dirent's version restarts at 1 when a name is
unlinked and recreated on a fresh ID, so `(name, version)` alone could name
different nodes at different times, whereas an unlink writes a tombstone to
the old dirent and so is reported as stale. Second, a path walk cites only
what it used: a write beneath `/a/b` cites the root, `a` and `b`, so write
cost grows with path depth rather than store size.

A vector cannot prove that a peer did not *add* an uncited entry during a
complete traversal. So after such a traversal the client sends a final cache
check with every version it saw, and if anything changed the traversal is
repeated, up to three times.

The agent's path cache stores the vector a lookup produced; a hit is not an
answer but a candidate that must be resubmitted to the server as a
precondition, and a refusal means the path must be walked again.

## Mutations

All namespace mutations are a `kvPut` of one or more dirents under a version
vector:

- **mkdir** creates a directory record with a random ID and seed, sends it
  with the parent's vector as precondition, then links a `Directory` dirent.
  Missing intermediate directories are created by the application layer one
  journaled step at a time, inheriting the item's read and write roles.
- **rm** rewrites the dirent with an all-zero node ID: a *tombstone*. A
  directory can only be unlinked recursively. The dirent's version advances,
  which is what makes the tombstone visible to any vector that cited it.
- **mv** is one `kvPut` carrying a tombstone at the source and a new dirent
  at the destination pointing at the *same* node ID. It reads the whole
  source subtree first to refuse moving a directory into itself, and cites
  the source's exact version so a concurrent change is rejected.
- **Overwrite** is permitted only from a file or small file to a file, small
  file, or symlink; a directory is never replaced by a put. An existing live
  entry is rejected unless the caller asked to overwrite, and the caller may
  supply an expected dirent version as a further precondition.

Every mutation is journaled before it is sent, using the intent log of
[Chapter 19](19-agent.qmd): exact request bytes in a
protected store first, then a public journal row that records `Prepared`,
`Submitting`, and, if the response is lost, `SubmissionUnknown`. An unknown
outcome is resolved by observation, never by resending: the client re-reads
the directory and finalises only when every prepared dirent appears with the
same client-authored bytes and MACs. An unacknowledged unlink cannot be
proven by absence, because absence is also what an unsent unlink looks like.

## The soft-state cache

Decrypted listings and file contents are kept in the client's soft-state
SQLite database, a cache that may be deleted at any time and rebuilt from
the network. Even a cache must not let a server roll the client's view
backwards. The projection refuses a root or directory with
a lower version than stored and refuses different bytes at the same version.
Two tables, `kv_directory_history` and `kv_entry_history`, hold
*ciphertext-only rollback anchors*: the last accepted version and encoded
bytes of each directory and entry. They survive permission-driven pruning,
so if a user loses read access to a subtree, its plaintext is dropped but
its anchors remain, and a later regrant cannot present an older directory as
current. Cached ciphertext goes through the same decode-and-authenticate
path as fresh bytes; a test flips a byte of it and checks the traversal
fails. Large files stream into SQLite in chunks rather than through memory;
the inline budget for one sync is 512 MiB.

## Quotas

The server enforces per-namespace limits by recomputing, on every write, the
namespace's total stored bytes and row count:

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Bytes per namespace | 16 GiB |
| Objects per namespace | 1,000,000 |
| Directories per namespace | 4,096 |
| Dirents per namespace | 100,000 |
| Encoded node size | 64 KiB |
| Encoded dirent size | 4,096 bytes |

The tree-shape limits are protocol constants the client also knows, and the
server refuses a configuration that would raise them above what a client
could synchronise. The server's documentation names the recomputed scan as
an expected saturation point.

## Why this design

Encrypting names only non-deterministically would make lookup cost
proportional to directory size and rule out server-side paging; encrypting
them deterministically under a key the server holds would leak equality
across the store and invite guessing. A per-directory keyed MAC beside a
randomised box gives the server a stable index it cannot invert, gives
listings a plaintext name, and confines equality leakage to one directory
version. The three-level hierarchy confines rotation cost to seed boxes, and
version vectors that cite IDs make "unchanged" mean unchanged.

## Where to look

- `foks-crypto`: `lib.rs` (`derive_kv_keys`, `KvKeySet`, the KV `seal_*`,
  `open_*` and `bind_*` functions, the typed secretbox and padding helpers).
- `foks-proto`: `kv.rs` (`KvRoot`, `KvDirectory`, `KvDirectoryPair`, `KvDirent`,
  `KvNodeId`, `KvPathVersionVector`, the protocol limits).
- `foks-client`: `kv/sync.rs` (traversal plans, listing, cache check,
  streaming downloads), `kv/write.rs` (root initialisation, mkdir, unlink,
  move, upload, the journaled namespace mutation and its reconciliation),
  `kv/support.rs`, `kv/mod.rs`.
- `foks-client-app`: `kv.rs` (path grammar, `mkdir -p`, store references).
- `foks-client-db`: `soft.rs` and `soft_schema.rs` (the projection, rollback
  anchors, large-file staging).
- `foks-server-db`: `kv.rs` (listing by MAC, version-vector checks, capacity
  accounting), `config.rs`.
- `foks-agent`: `read_cache.rs` (remembered path vectors).
